sourceNote: Reviewed all supplied events E0–E3796. Attribution follows conversational turns, not ideological content. The transcript contains transcription errors and several events combining speakers; these are marked U where inseparable. No audio or external sources were consulted. No edited teaser replays were identified.

candidates.speaker: A
candidates.quote: God could always create a world with more or less suffering.
candidates.explanation: The proposed adjustment of goods alongside any amount of suffering could insulate the claim from contrary patterns (E1175–1182). However, Horn explicitly conditions justification on greater good and supplies functional and ethical examples (E1157–1172, E1195–1220). Whether this licenses unrestricted compensation rather than a contestable conditional argument remains unclear.

candidates.speaker: A
candidates.quote: I do not believe unjustified suffering exists at all
candidates.explanation: Asked whether unjustified suffering exists, Horn rules it out because any suffering can be justified through greater goods or prevented evils (E2099–2105). The missing bridge is from possible justification to its universal actuality. This protects against contrary suffering patterns, though he subsequently preserves distinctions between evil, toleration, and forbidden actions (E2118–2126).

candidates.speaker: A
candidates.quote: I don't really have epistemic access to all of them because I'm a limited finite creature
candidates.explanation: In response to the specific extent of animal suffering, inaccessible divine reasons widen the proposed justification beyond what can be examined (E2275–2284). Yet Horn offers a human analogy and the goodness of animal existence (E2269–2292). The passage does not clearly establish whether unknown reasons defeat every objection or merely support a limited possibility.

candidates.speaker: A
candidates.quote: any evil that he allows to exist uh will be justified
candidates.explanation: The universal justification could neutralize every contrary instance of evil, without identifying its compensating good (E2831–2838). Here, however, Horn explicitly frames it conditionally on God's perfect morality and supports the permission principle with roads and free speech (E2839–2846). Its use as unconditional protection rather than a conditional consequence is uncertain.

candidates.speaker: A
candidates.quote: But if I threw God out of the picture all I'd be left with is the horrid evils.
candidates.explanation: The loss of hoped-for compensation becomes a reason to retain belief unless further evidence appears (E3491–3503), without establishing that comforting compensation exists. However, Horn is describing his personal response, acknowledges intellectual difficulties (E3456–3459), and allows incoherence or failed arguments to change his position. Neither proof substitution nor unrestricted protection is established.

candidates.speaker: A
candidates.quote: remember that you are made in God's image. You are loved.
candidates.explanation: The affirmation grounds a call for respectful conduct in divine love, creation, and everlasting worth (E3578–3591). Earlier moral arguments support part of that framework, but everlasting life receives no comparable defense. Because this also functions as a closing pastoral exhortation, its use as a replacement for public proof remains uncertain; disagreement is not discredited.

contrasts.speaker: A
contrasts.quote: if the demonstrative arguments for God's existence work then no probabilistic argument from evil can overcome them.
contrasts.explanation: Horn explicitly conditions the conclusion on the arguments working, applies the same rule to a hypothetical proof against God (E3243–3246), and requests consideration of all evidence. This qualification prevents treating the repeated formulation itself as unconditional immunity from criticism.

contrasts.speaker: B
contrasts.quote: It's that animals are worth more than human taste buds.
contrasts.explanation: The memorable formulation summarizes a distinction supported by discussion of differing capacities for pleasure and unequal moral weight. O'Connor expressly denies that opposing animal suffering requires equal human and animal worth, and explains why different judgments about mass killing remain compatible.
